title: Letter sounds s-a-t-p-i-n
keywords: s a t p i n
examples: Teacher, what sound does the letter 's' make?
Can you show me how to make the sound for 'a'?
Where is the letter 't' on the chart?

explain.say: Let us learn the pure sounds for these letters today. We will say the sound clearly for each letter.

draw.text: s a t p i n

explain.say: For the letter s, say /s/ like a snake. Keep your mouth in a small, straight line.
For the letter a, say /a/ like when you open your mouth wide. Your mouth makes a small triangle shape.
Now for the letter t, say /t/ with a quick puff of air. Your tongue taps behind your top teeth.
For the letter p, say /p/ with a little burst of air. Your lips come together and then pop open.
A common mistake is saying the letter name instead of the sound. Remember we are making the sound, not saying the letter name. Say /s/ like a quiet hiss, not 'ess'.

faq.q: Why do I not say 'uh' when I say the sound for 'a'?
faq.a: The pure sound for 'a' is a short, quick sound. It is not the sound you make when you say 'uh'.
asks: What is the right sound for 'a'?
Should I add an extra sound to 'a'?

faq.q: How do I know if my mouth shape is correct for 's'?
faq.a: Try making the sound while looking in a mirror. Your mouth should look like a thin, straight line.
asks: What does my mouth look like for 's'?
Can you check my mouth shape for 's'?

faq.q: Is the sound for 't' the same as the sound for 'd'?
faq.a: No, the sound for 't' is a quick puff of air. The sound for 'd' uses your tongue touching your teeth.
asks: What is the difference between 't' and 'd' sounds?
How do I make the 't' sound?

faq.q: If I see the letter 'p', what sound should I make?
faq.a: You should make a short, popping sound. It is like blowing a little puff of air.
asks: Say the sound for this letter.

faq.q: Do I need to use my hands when I make the letter sounds?
faq.a: No, for these pure sounds, we only use our mouths and tongues. Our hands stay still.
asks: Do I move my body for phonics?
Is it okay to use my hands?

facts: Phonics teaches the relationship between letters and sounds.
Pure sounds are the short, clear sounds that each letter makes.
The letter 's' makes a /s/ sound, like a snake.
The letter 'a' makes a short /a/ sound, like in apple.

quiz.say: What sound does the letter 't' make?
quiz.why: The sound for 't' is a quick puff of air made by tapping your tongue.

wrong.0: This is wrong because /a/ is the sound for the letter 'a'.
wrong.2: This is tempting because 'd' and 't' are both sounds made with the tongue.
wrong.3: This is wrong because /s/ is the sound for the letter 's'.

quiz.say: If I see the letter 'p', what sound should I make?
quiz.why: The sound for 'p' is a short burst of air that pops out of your lips.

wrong.0: This is wrong because we want the pure sound, not a drawn-out sound.
wrong.2: This is tempting because 'b' and 'p' both use your lips.
wrong.3: This is wrong because /t/ uses your tongue, not just your lips.

quiz.say: What sound does the letter 's' make?
quiz.why: The sound for 's' is a smooth, hissing sound, like a snake.

wrong.1: This is wrong because /z/ is a different buzzing sound.
wrong.2: This is wrong because we need the pure sound, not a drawn-out sound.
wrong.3: This is wrong because we should not add an extra vowel sound at the end.
